ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a connected patch of shaded identical equilateral unit triangles arranged on a triangular grid. Counting the shaded unit triangles in the patch gives 7 already placed little triangles. Reasoning: The smallest complete equilateral triangle on the same triangular grid that can contain this whole patch must have side length 4 unit-triangle edges; a side length 3 triangle is too small to cover the left-to-right and downward spread of the shown arrangement. A complete equilateral triangle of side length n contains n^2 unit triangles, so side length 4 contains 4^2 = 16 little triangles. Clara has already placed 7, so she must add 16 - 7 = 9 little triangles.

method.method_draft: First describe the diagram as a patch of shaded identical equilateral unit triangles on a triangular grid. Count the shaded unit triangles already present in the patch: there are 7. Then determine the smallest complete equilateral triangle on this same grid that can contain the whole patch without moving or rotating individual pieces; the outermost occupied positions force a side length of 4 little-triangle edges, since a side length 3 triangle cannot span the shown left-to-right/downward arrangement. Use the rule that a large equilateral triangle of side length n made from unit equilateral triangles contains n^2 little triangles. Thus the smallest possible big triangle has 4^2 = 16 little triangles, so Clara must add 16 - 7 = 9.
